fields.sample_size: documentary and secondary-data analysis: IBGE 2010 Census and DataSUS (Tabnet) data by colour/race; 231,087 deaths from diseases related to inadequate environmental sanitation 1996-2014 (77% with race recorded: 55% Black, 43% white)
fields.effect_estimate: In the 2010 Census, 61% of the population without water supply was Black (37% white), 67% of those without waste collection was Black (30% white) and 58% of those without sewage treatment was Black (40% white), against 51% Black and 48% white in the population; the author estimates a Black person dies every hour and a half from lack of sanitation and frames this as the result of State, institutional racism and environmental racism from colonial Brazil onward. Deaths data have 23% missing race; the hourly figure is an extrapolation from the DataSUS counts and uses a rhetorical aeroplane metaphor. Calls for race-disaggregated public databases. Descriptive; no tests.
fields.study_design: exploratory bibliographic research with descriptive analysis of census and mortality data by colour/race
fields.section: Full text: Method; institutional racism and sanitation; Colonial continuum; current data (Census 2010, DataSUS); Final considerations
fields.exact_location: Method; institutional racism and sanitation; Colonial continuum; current data (Census 2010, DataSUS); Final considerations

evidence_level: Single-study evidence: an exploratory bibliographic and descriptive-data paper on racial inequality in Brazilian sanitation and sanitation-related deaths, read in full text 2026-10-04. Black people are over-represented among those lacking water, waste collection and sewage treatment (61%, 67%, 58% vs 51% of the population). Descriptive, no inferential tests.
notes: Abstract-level extraction accurate; adds the census percentages. The causal framing (genocide, institutional racism) is interpretive. Legal/administrative exposure is the State's provision of services, not a specific rule.
